content: The use of clinical decision support systems (CDSS) on handheld devices at the point of care, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, has the potential to improve adherence to treatment protocols and patient outcomes. However, the evidence regarding the impact of CDSS on mobile devices remains limited and inconclusive. To address this gap, the World Health Organization (WHO) is developing guidelines to guide investments in digital decision support tools to strengthen primary healthcare. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of digital clinical decision support tools accessible via mobile devices for primary healthcare providers in primary care settings. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, Global Health Library, and others, up to July 19, 2017. Additional searches included the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, the US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register, and Epistemonikos for related systematic reviews and eligible primary studies. Studies published after 2000 in any language were considered. The selection criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving healthcare providers, including lay health workers and other staff involved in primary healthcare delivery using clinical decision support tools. Studies involving patients receiving care from such providers were also included. Interventions compared digital clinical decision support tools accessible via mobile devices with non-digital tools or no interventions. Mobile devices included mobile phones, tablets, personal digital assistants, and smartphones, but not laptops or analog landline telephones. Studies where digital tools were integrated with electronic medical records or other longitudinal tracking systems were excluded. Data collection and analysis involved screening search results using a machine learning classifier to identify RCTs. Titles and abstracts with a 10% probability of being RCTs were screened by two reviewers, while those with less than 10% probability were screened by one reviewer. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were conducted independently by two authors. Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RR) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MD) were calculated for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, and a Summary of Findings was prepared. Due to differences in interventions and outcome measures, meta-analysis was not performed. Main Results: Five RCTs met the inclusion criteria. Three trials were conducted in the United States, one in India, and one in both India and China. The intervention may increase the number of individuals with high cardiovascular disease risk taking aspirin (low certainty evidence). The intervention probably increases the number of individuals taking their antihypertensive medication (moderate certainty evidence). The intervention probably makes little or no difference to the number of individuals with hyperlipidemia reaching LDL cholesterol goals or to systolic blood pressure levels among individuals with high cardiovascular disease risk (moderate certainty evidence). The intervention may make little or no difference to medication adherence, HbA1c levels, or satisfaction with the helpfulness or clarity of medication information among individuals with poorly controlled diabetes (low certainty evidence). The effect of the intervention on providers’ adherence to recommended clinical practice, providers’ acceptability or satisfaction, quality of data about services provided, resource use, utilization of healthcare services, and unintended consequences is uncertain due to very low certainty evidence or lack of direct evidence. Authors’ Conclusions: The review provides limited evidence that clinical decision support interventions delivered using mobile devices can improve outcomes in primary healthcare settings. Moderate-quality evidence suggests that the use of mobile CDSS may improve medication adherence among patients, but this adherence may not translate into significant improvements in patient health outcomes. Further high-quality trials are needed to robustly establish the effects of mobile CDSS interventions. Summary of Findings: Patient or Population: Healthcare providers using clinical decision support tools and patients receiving care from such providers. Setting: Primary healthcare settings (India, China, USA). Intervention: Mobile clinical decision support system. Comparison: Standard care or no intervention (e.g., paper-based tools, provider training, or usual care without additional follow-up). Outcomes: 1. Providers’ adherence to recommended practice: Very low certainty evidence; effect uncertain. 2. Time between presentation and appropriate management: No studies identified; effect uncertain. 3. Utilization of healthcare services: No studies identified; effect uncertain. 4. Resource use: No studies identified; effect uncertain. 5. Unintended consequences: No studies identified; effect uncertain. GRADE Definitions: High certainty: Very confident that the true effect is close to the estimate. Moderate certainty: Moderately confident; the true effect is likely close to the estimate but may differ substantially. Low certainty: Limited confidence; the true effect may differ substantially from the estimate. Very low certainty: Very little confidence; the true effect is likely substantially different from the estimate.
